title: Question 5
stem:
Fig. 5.1 shows a pendulum consisting of a metal sphere suspended by a thin string.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1 (not to scale)

The sphere undergoes small oscillations about its equilibrium position. The oscillations may be considered to be simple harmonic.

Fig. 5.2 shows the variation with time $t$ of the displacement $x$ of the sphere from its equilibrium position.

{{figure:figure_5_2}}

Fig. 5.2

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: On Fig. 5.1, draw an arrow, from the centre of the sphere, to represent the direction of the resultant force acting on the sphere when it is in the position shown.

markscheme_points.text: arrow from sphere, perpendicular to string, pointing left and down

hints: Hint 1: Think about where the equilibrium position is for this pendulum and which way the sphere must be pulled back toward it when it is displaced to the right as shown.
parts.proper_answer: Arrow drawn from centre of sphere, directed to the left and down, perpendicular to the string (tangential to the arc, towards equilibrium).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the restoring effect**
You are looking at a pendulum pulled to one side. In SHM the resultant force is always a restoring force, so it must act to pull the sphere back toward its equilibrium position at the bottom of the swing.

Step 2: **Get the direction right**
The sphere can only move along the circular arc. So the component that causes motion is tangential to the arc, which is perpendicular to the string. From the position shown on the right, that is down and to the left.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: The mass of the sphere is $0.15\text{kg}$.
parts.text: State the amplitude of the oscillations.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 5.2 and focus on the largest distance the $x$ trace reaches away from $x = 0$, checking the $x$-axis scale carefully.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember what amplitude means**
Amplitude $x_0$ is the maximum magnitude of displacement from equilibrium, not peak-to-peak. On an $x-t$ graph it is simply the height of a peak above zero or depth of a trough below zero.

Step 2: **Read it from Fig. 5.2**
The peaks reach to $0.016\text{ m}$ and the troughs to $-0.016\text{ m}$. So $$x_0 = 0.016\text{ m}$$

key_concepts: amplitude as maximum displacement from equilibrium

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the angular frequency of the oscillations.
hints: Hint 1: Start from Fig. 5.2 by finding the time for one complete oscillation, for example from one peak to the next peak.
Hint 2: Think about how angular frequency $\omega$ is linked to that repeat time $T$ for a sine or cosine oscillation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the period T from the graph**
One full cycle is peak to peak. Peaks are at $t = 0.40\text{ s}$ and $t = 0.80\text{ s}$, so $$T = 0.80 - 0.40 = 0.40\text{ s}$$ You can check with troughs or any repeating point and get the same.

Step 2: **Convert period to angular frequency**
For SHM: $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ So $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{0.40} \approx 16\text{ rad s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the total energy of the oscillations.
hints: Hint 1: Recall that total energy in SHM is constant and equals the kinetic energy at the centre ($x = 0$) or the potential energy at the amplitude, involving $m$, $\omega$ and $x_0$.
Hint 2: Check you have all three numbers ready in SI units: $m = 0.15\text{ kg}$ plus your $\omega$ and $x_0$ from the last two parts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the energy formula**
Total mechanical energy is conserved and is: $$E = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x_0^2$$ This is also $\frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^2$ since $v_{max} = \omega x_0$.

Step 2: **Substitute and calculate**
Using $m = 0.15\text{ kg}$, $\omega = 15.7\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ and $x_0 = 0.016\text{ m}$: $$E = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.15 \times (15.7)^2 \times (0.016)^2 \approx 4.7 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$$

parts.label: (c)

markscheme_points.text: dome-shaped curve starting and ending on the x-axis, with peak at x = 0
minimum x shown as −0.016 m and maximum x shown as +0.016 m at the ends of the line

hints: Hint 1: Think about the speed of the sphere at the centre ($x = 0$) compared with at the turning points ($x = \pm x_0$) and what that means for $E_K$.
Hint 2: Recall the shape of $E_K$ against $x$ for SHM - it is not a straight line, but a curve that is symmetric about $x = 0$.
Hint 3: Plan the key numbers to label on your axes using your answers for amplitude and total energy, noting the $E_K$ axis is in units of $10^{-3}\text{ J}$.
parts.proper_answer: Inverted parabola (dome) with $E_K = 0$ at $x = \pm 0.016\text{ m}$ and maximum $E_K = 4.7 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$ at $x = 0$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Think physically about KE**
At the equilibrium $x = 0$ the sphere is fastest, so $E_K$ is maximum and equals the total energy. At the extremes $x = \pm x_0$ it momentarily stops, so $E_K = 0$. That already tells you the curve must start on the $x$-axis, rise to a peak in the middle, then fall back to the axis.

Step 2: **Recall the mathematical shape**
Since $E_K = E_{total} - E_P$ and $E_P \propto x^2$, the $E_K$ - $x$ graph is an inverted parabola: $$E_K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2(x_0^2 - x^2)$$ It is symmetric about $x = 0$.

Step 3: **Add the correct labels**
Sketch a smooth dome from $x = -0.016\text{ m}$ to $x = +0.016\text{ m}$ on the $x$-axis, peaking at $x = 0$ with $$E_{K,max} = 4.7 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$$ which is $4.7$ on the $E_K / 10^{-3}\text{ J}$ axis.
